source.title: Sublethal neonicotinoid exposure reduces homing success in free-flying honeybee foragers: a radio-frequency identification field experiment
source.abstract: Concern about pollinator decline has focused on sublethal effects of systemic insecticides that do not kill bees outright. We fitted 960 honeybee foragers from three apiaries in southern England with 2.4 mg radio-frequency identification tags and released them 1 km from their hives. Half of the bees had been fed a single 1.5 ng dose of a neonicotinoid, a quantity consistent with residues measured in oilseed rape nectar in the same region. Antennal readers at each hive entrance logged every return. Homing success was 71% in the exposed group and 84% in the untreated control group, a difference of 13 percentage points (p = 0.002). Returning exposed bees took a median of 8 minutes longer. Colony weight and brood area were monitored for eight weeks after the experiment and no colony failed during that period. The experiment was conducted in a single season and we did not test repeated exposure.
source.tldr: Bees given a field-realistic dose of a neonicotinoid were less likely to find their way home, though no colonies collapsed during the study.
source.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
